order: keep them to show a grown-up
safety: never share someone's photo without asking
you are never to blame for someone else's unkindness

little.twist: A new story: a friend says you can't play. And four slow breaths.
little.can_now: name a feeling, calm down with slow balloon breaths and by noticing what they see, and ask a trusted grown-up for help

steps.say: This is the Calm Corner: a quiet place to practise feeling calm. Everyone has big feelings sometimes. Nothing you pick here is kept.
Bobo's tower fell down. Look at Bobo's face. How does Bobo feel?

choices.why: Look again: Bobo's mouth turns down and the eyes look down. Bobo feels sad.
Look again: Bobo's mouth turns down and the eyes look down. Bobo feels sad.

steps.done: Sad. Naming a feeling is the first step to feeling better.

steps.say: How do you feel right now? Any answer is fine.

choices.reply: It's OK to feel sad. Let's breathe together.
It's OK to feel cross. Let's breathe together.
It's OK to feel worried. Let's breathe together.

steps.say: Balloon breathing: breathe in slowly while the balloon grows, then out slowly while it shrinks. Three times.
steps.done: Slow breaths. Your body feels calmer.

steps.say: Balloon breathing: in slowly while the balloon grows, out slowly while it shrinks. Four times.
steps.done: Four slow breaths. Calm.

steps.say: Bobo breathed with you. Look: Bobo's face is calm now.
Look all around the room. Find five things you can see.
steps.done: Five things! Noticing what is around you helps your mind feel calm.

steps.say: Is anything worrying you? Pick a picture. You don't have to say more.
Put the worry in the worry box. Later, you can take it out and talk about it with a grown-up you trust.
steps.done: In the box. Worries get smaller when we share them.

steps.say: Look: Mo and Bobo are playing ball. Pip-pop is all on her own and looks sad.
What could you do?

choices.why: Being left out feels sad. Asking someone to join in is kind.

steps.done: Pip-pop joins in. Everyone smiles.

steps.say: A new story: Mo says to you, "You can't play with us." How might that feel?
What could you do?

choices.text: Say how I feel, find someone else to play with, and tell a grown-up

choices.why: Pushing hurts and makes things worse. Say how you feel, play with someone else, and tell a grown-up.

steps.done: Calm words, a new friend to play with, and a grown-up who can help.

steps.say: When you feel sad or worried, who can you tell?

choices.why: Telling a grown-up you trust helps. You don't have to keep a worry on your own.

steps.done: A grown-up you trust: at home, or at school.

steps.say: You named feelings, breathed slowly, looked around, put a worry away and helped a friend. The Calm Corner is always here.

check.say: Bobo's mouth turns down. Bobo feels...
You feel cross. What can help you calm down?
Someone is left out. You can...
A worry won't go away. Who can you tell?

name_it.title: Name it, calm it
lines: Name the feeling: sad, cross, worried, happy...
Breathe slowly: in like a balloon, out slowly.
Look around: find five things you can see.
Share a worry with a grown-up you trust.
name_it.source: CASEL's social and emotional learning (self-awareness, self-management) and UNICEF's advice for children

little.try_real: Teach your grown-up balloon breathing: breathe in while your hands rise, out while they fall. Make a worry box at home together.

sources.fact: Self-awareness (identifying one's emotions) and self-management (managing emotions, using stress-management strategies) are core social and emotional competencies; so is seeking or offering help.
Slow, deep breathing in and out can calm the body when you feel stressed or anxious.
Children feel better when they talk to an adult they trust about their worries; sharing a worry makes it smaller.
Inclusion and kindness: inviting a child who is left out is a simple way to help.
sources.source: UNICEF, how to talk to your children about bullying

middle.twist: The unkindness is online too: a mean message about Pip-pop.
middle.can_now: use a calm toolbox (breathing, counting, a walk, talking), say how they feel calmly, solve a quarrel fairly, and know what to do when someone is unkind

steps.say: The Calm Corner. Today: a toolbox of calm, and some tricky moments with friends. Nothing you pick here is kept.
Bobo and Mo both want the ball. Look at their faces. How do they feel?

choices.why: Look at their eyebrows and mouths: they both feel cross.

steps.done: Cross. Big feelings: first, calm down.

steps.say: Stop and breathe with them: slowly in while the balloon grows, slowly out. Four times.
steps.done: Calmer. Now we can think.

steps.say: The calm toolbox: pick three tools that help you calm down.
steps.done: Your own toolbox: use it whenever a feeling gets big.

steps.say: Bobo wants to tell Mo how it feels. Which words help?

choices.text: "I feel cross when you take the ball."

choices.why: Shouting makes the other person cross too. Say how you feel, calmly: "I feel... when..."

steps.done: "I feel... when...": calm words, clear words.

steps.say: Now they listen to each other. What is a fair way?

choices.why: Grabbing isn't fair. Taking turns, or playing together, is.

steps.done: Turns! They play together again.

steps.say: In the playground, Mo says something unkind to Pip-pop. Pip-pop looks upset. What can you do?

choices.text: Stay with Pip-pop and tell a grown-up

choices.why: Laughing along hurts Pip-pop more. Stay with her, and tell a grown-up.
Pip-pop needs a friend. Stay with her and tell a grown-up.

steps.done: Being a kind friend, and getting help: brave.

steps.say: On the tablet, someone sends a mean message about Pip-pop. What do you do?

choices.text: Don't reply, keep it, show a grown-up

choices.why: A mean reply makes it worse. Don't reply: keep the message and show a grown-up you trust.

steps.done: No reply. A grown-up can help block and report it.

steps.say: With your grown-up, press BLOCK.
steps.done: Blocked: they can't message you now.

steps.say: Who can help when someone is unkind?

choices.text: A teacher or a grown-up I trust

choices.why: Grown-ups can help: a parent, a teacher, someone at school. Keep telling until someone helps.

steps.done: Keep telling until someone helps.

steps.say: How do you feel after practising? Any answer is fine.

choices.reply: That's OK. Use your toolbox, and talk to a grown-up you trust.

steps.say: You calmed down with your toolbox, said how you feel, found a fair way, and stood by a friend. Those are real skills.

check.say: A feeling is getting big. First you...
Which words help in a quarrel?
Two friends want the same ball. A fair way is...
Someone is unkind to a friend. You...

choices.text: Stay with them, tell a grown-up

name_it.title: The calm toolbox
lines: Use your tools: count to ten, walk, talk, draw.
Find a fair way: take turns, listen.
Unkindness: stay with your friend, tell a grown-up you trust.
name_it.source: CASEL's social and emotional learning, and anti-bullying advice (UNICEF, StopBullying.gov)

middle.try_real: Make your calm toolbox at home: draw your three tools on a card and keep it in your bag. Tell your grown-up which ones you picked.

sources.fact: Relationship skills include communicating clearly, listening, cooperating and resolving conflicts constructively; responsible decision-making considers what is fair.
When you see bullying: be there for the person, don't join in, and tell a trusted adult.
sources.source: StopBullying.gov (US Department of Health and Human Services)

sources.fact: Cyberbullying: don't respond, keep the evidence, block the person, report it, and talk to someone you trust.
sources.source: UNICEF, cyberbullying: what is it and how to stop it

sources.fact: Slow, deep breathing can calm the body when you feel stressed.

big.twist: The pressure grows: a whole group chat laughs at a post, and you are asked to add to it.
big.can_now: say no to pressure, deal with online unkindness (don't reply, keep it, block, report, tell), calm a stressed body, and know when and where to get help

steps.say: The Calm Corner. Today: pressure from friends, being unkind online, and knowing where to get help. Nothing you pick here is kept.
Friends say: share this silly photo of Mo, everyone will laugh. Mo didn't say yes. What do you do?

choices.text: Say no: I don't share it

choices.why: Sharing someone's photo without asking can hurt them a lot. You can say no, even to friends.

steps.done: No is a strong word. Real friends accept it.

steps.say: How might Mo feel if it was shared?

choices.why: Imagine it was your photo. Mo would probably feel hurt and embarrassed.

steps.done: Thinking how others feel helps you choose well.

steps.say: A whole group chat is laughing at a post about Mo, and they ask you to add a joke. What do you do?

choices.text: Don't add to it; tell Mo you're there, tell a trusted adult

choices.why: Even if everyone is, adding to it hurts Mo more. Stay out of it, support Mo, and tell a trusted adult.

steps.done: Standing apart from a crowd takes courage.

steps.say: Now someone sends YOU a mean message. It is never your fault. Here is what to do.
First: should you reply?

choices.why: A reply gives them what they want and makes it bigger. Don't reply.

steps.done: No reply.

steps.say: Should you delete it straight away?

choices.text: Keep it to show a trusted adult

choices.why: Keep it (a screenshot) so a trusted adult can see it and help report it.

steps.done: Kept, to show someone who can help.

steps.say: Press BLOCK.
steps.done: Blocked.

steps.say: Press REPORT, so the app knows.
steps.done: Reported.

steps.say: Messages like that can make your heart race. Breathe slowly: in for four, out for four. Four times.
steps.done: A slower heart, a clearer mind.

steps.say: Bring your mind back to the room: find five things you can see.
steps.done: Back in the here and now.

steps.say: When should you get help from an adult?

choices.text: A worry that won't go away, or someone hurting me

choices.why: Everyone needs help sometimes. Asking for help is brave, not weak.

steps.done: Asking for help is brave.

steps.say: Where: a parent or carer, a teacher, a school counsellor, a doctor. Many countries have a free children's helpline too. Keep telling until someone helps.
How do you feel after practising? Any answer is fine.

choices.reply: Strong! You know what to do.
That's OK. Talk to an adult you trust about it.

steps.say: You said no to pressure, handled a mean message, calmed your body and know where help is. That is strength.

check.say: Friends push you to share someone's photo. You...
Someone sends you a mean message. First...
A mean message: keep it or delete it?

choices.text: Keep it to show an adult

check.say: Asking an adult for help is...

name_it.title: Pressure, and getting help
lines: You can say no to pressure, even to friends.
Unkind online: don't reply, keep it, block, report.
Calm your body: slow breaths, notice five things.
Tell an adult you trust. Keep telling until someone helps.
name_it.source: UNICEF's cyberbullying advice, CASEL's social and emotional learning, and Child Helpline International

big.try_real: With your grown-up, find the BLOCK and REPORT buttons in an app you use, and write down who you can talk to: at home, at school, and your country's children's helpline.

sources.fact: If you are cyberbullied: don't respond, keep the evidence (screenshots), block the person, report it on the platform, and talk to someone you trust.
sources.source: UNICEF, cyberbullying: what is it and how to stop it

sources.fact: Responsible decision-making and relationship skills include resisting negative social pressure and seeking help when needed.
Free child helplines exist in more than 130 countries; Child Helpline International lists them.
Slow breathing (for example in for a count of four, out for a count of four) can calm stress.
